blocks.content: The least privilege principle is the single idea tying together every topic in this module: grant a container only the access it genuinely needs to do its job, and nothing more.

Least privilege is not a Docker-specific idea, it is a foundational security concept applied here: every permission, every capability, every piece of access a container has should exist because the application genuinely needs it, not because it was simply the default.

blocks.alt: Grant exactly what is needed, nothing left over "just in case"

blocks.content: 2. Every Earlier Topic Is an Application of This
blocks.text: 2. Every Earlier Topic Is an Application of This

blocks.content: Looking back across this module, every technique covered so far is really the same principle applied to a different resource: a non-root USER limits what the process itself can do, a read-only filesystem limits what it can persist, a minimal base image limits what is even present to exploit, and file-based secrets limit who can read sensitive values.

blocks.alt: Four earlier topics, one underlying principle

blocks.content: Beyond user and filesystem permissions, a container by default still has a broad set of Linux capabilities (fine-grained kernel privileges) it likely does not need. --cap-drop ALL, followed by explicitly adding back only what is genuinely required, is least privilege applied directly at the kernel capability level.

blocks.alt: Start from nothing, add back only what is genuinely needed

blocks.content:
docker run --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE myapp
# Drops every capability, then adds back only the one needed
# to bind a privileged port.

code.content:

# Drops every capability, then adds back only the one needed
# to bind a privileged port.

docker run --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE myapp
# Drops every capability, then adds back only the one needed
# to bind a privileged port.

blocks.content: --privileged disables nearly every security boundary Docker normally provides, essentially the opposite of least privilege. It should be treated as a last resort for a genuinely unavoidable use case, never a default reached for out of convenience.

blocks.alt: The furthest thing from least privilege, avoided unless truly unavoidable

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Least privilege is the unifying idea behind every technique in this module, grant only the access a container genuinely needs.
Applied concretely: a non-root user, a read-only filesystem, a minimal base image, file-based secrets, dropped capabilities, and avoiding --privileged entirely.
